scr_ap_what_you_can_edit_on_an_a_p_invoi.purpose: Sets out, state by state, which fields on an A/P invoice remain editable — full edit while the invoice is a draft, partial edit (invoice number, terms, memo) once it is approved or posted, and nothing at all once a check has cleared against it.
scr_ap_what_you_can_edit_on_an_a_p_invoi.outcome: Editors know before they open an invoice whether a correction can be typed in or needs a credit memo and re-entry, so the approved amount is never silently changed after sign-off.
scr_ap_what_you_can_edit_on_an_a_p_invoi.rootCause: An approval signature only means something if the thing approved cannot be edited afterwards. RealPage narrows the editable field set as an invoice advances so that the amount and GL coding an approver saw are frozen at approval; without that lock an approver's electronic sign-off would be worthless as SOC 1 evidence.
scr_ap_what_you_can_edit_on_an_a_p_invoi.ifSkipped: Staff change amounts or GL coding on already-approved invoices, and the approval audit trail no longer describes the invoice that was actually paid.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, authorization and change control
ASC 405-10 — recognition of liabilities
SOC 1 — completeness and accuracy of approved transactions
redFlags: Amount or GL account changed on an invoice already carrying an approval
Staff granted full-edit rights on posted invoices to 'save time'
Corrections made by edit rather than by credit memo when the period is closed
scr_ap_what_you_can_edit_on_an_a_p_invoi.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Payables > Payable Entry — the payable locks progressively as it moves through PAYscan workflow; post-approval corrections are made by a negative payable rather than by editing.

scr_ap_future_draft_invoice_notification.purpose: Describes the automated email RealPage sends to the person who saved or submitted an invoice when posting it generates a future-dated draft journal entry, naming the journal and transaction number so the draft is not forgotten in a later period.
scr_ap_future_draft_invoice_notification.outcome: The submitter is told in writing that a second, future-period entry is sitting in draft and must be activated, so the deferred half of the transaction actually posts.
scr_ap_future_draft_invoice_notification.rootCause: Invoices that straddle periods — an annual insurance premium or a prepaid service contract — create a companion draft entry dated in a future month. Nothing in the current-month close touches that draft, so without a notification the amortization simply never posts and 1310 Prepaid Expenses sits overstated for the rest of the year.
scr_ap_future_draft_invoice_notification.ifSkipped: Future-period draft entries stay unactivated, prepaid balances never amortize, and monthly operating expense is understated until someone rolls forward the prepaid schedule.
gaap: ASC 340-10 — deferred costs and prepaid expense amortization
COSO 2013 — Principle 16, ongoing monitoring of automated notifications
redFlags: Notifications addressed to a departed employee's mailbox
Draft entries older than one closed period still unactivated
Prepaid rollforward that does not agree to the outstanding draft entries
scr_ap_future_draft_invoice_notification.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Financials > Recurring Journal Entry with a future start period, plus Tools > Post Recurring Journal Entries; Voyager notifies via workflow task rather than a draft-JE email.

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.purpose: Opens the Available budget panel from the Spend control button while a subcontract is being written, showing the job cost budget remaining before the contract value is committed — with an over-budget line shown red and parenthesized in the Remaining column.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.outcome: The contract writer sees the job's uncommitted budget before signing, so a subcontract is not executed for more than the owner funded.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.rootCause: A subcontract is a binding commitment for the full contract value, not a request; once executed the owner owes the balance whether or not budget exists. Checking available budget at creation is the only point where the number can still be renegotiated, because after execution the remedy is a funded change order or an owner capital call.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.ifSkipped: Subcontracts are signed above the funded job budget, and the overrun surfaces only when pay applications start hitting 1410 Construction in Progress with no budget line to absorb them.
gaap: ASC 440-10 — unrecorded commitments
ASC 360-10-30 — costs capitalized into long-lived assets
Construction loan agreement approved-budget covenants
redFlags: Contract value exceeding the funded line with no contingency transfer
Budget check run against a stale, unpublished budget version
Subcontract executed before the lender approved the revised project budget
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.yardi: Yardi Voyager Job Cost: Contract entry with budget validation against the job budget; over-budget contracts flagged in Job Cost > Budget Comparison.

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.purpose: Shows the Available budget page from within purchase order entry, presenting Month, Year to date and Current year tabs for standard line items or the job cost budget when job cost lines were chosen, so the buyer sees the remaining amount before committing the PO.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.outcome: The purchase order is written against a budget line the buyer has actually looked at, with the period basis — month versus year — made explicit.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.rootCause: Property managers commit spend under delegated authority but rarely hold the budget open beside them. The month tab and the year-to-date tab can disagree sharply on a seasonal account such as 6210 Utilities or 6110 Repairs & Maintenance, and a buyer who reads only the annual figure commits against budget that later months need.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.ifSkipped: POs are raised against budget that is annually available but monthly exhausted, and the property runs a variance the regional manager must explain with no advance warning.
gaap: ASC 440-10 — purchase commitments
COSO 2013 — Principle 10, control activities over authorization
redFlags: Buyers relying on the Current year tab when the spend is monthly
Budget check excluding unapproved invoices already in the queue
POs split below the threshold to avoid the budget warning
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.yardi: Yardi Procure to Pay: PO Entry with budget validation by GL account and period; Financial Analytics > Budget Comparison for the underlying budget.

scr_ap_why_you_cant_find_the_reclassify_.purpose: Troubleshoots a missing Reclassify link on invoices by pointing to the two causes — the Accounts Receivable configuration flag 'Enable reclassification for invoices and adjustments' being off, or the user lacking edit-and-reclassify permission in both the A/R and A/P permission sets.
scr_ap_why_you_cant_find_the_reclassify_.outcome: The accountant learns whether the block is a company configuration switch or their own permission set, and knows which administrator request to raise.
scr_ap_why_you_cant_find_the_reclassify_.rootCause: Reclassification is deliberately gated because it moves a posted expense between GL accounts and properties after approval. When the option silently disappears, accountants work around it with manual journal entries that leave the A/P subledger detail pointing at the original wrong account, and invoice-level support no longer matches the ledger.
scr_ap_why_you_cant_find_the_reclassify_.ifSkipped: Miscoded invoices are corrected by side journal entries, so the A/P detail and the GL tell different stories and owner variance commentary cannot be traced back to the vendor invoice.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 11, controls over technology access
Treas. Reg. §1.263(a)-3 — capital versus repair determination
SOC 1 — logical access controls
redFlags: Reclassify permission granted broadly to avoid support tickets
Manual journal entries used in place of reclass, breaking the subledger link
Reclass enabled without a compensating review of posted reclasses
scr_ap_why_you_cant_find_the_reclassify_.yardi: Yardi Voyager: payable reclass requires the Payables 'Reclass' function right in the user role; otherwise corrections run through Financials > Journal Entry.

scr_ap_setting_a_system_action_when_a_tr.purpose: Configures, per transaction type, whether RealPage warns the user or outright prevents saving when an A/P invoice or purchase order would push a GL account over budget, and whether the check measures against the current posting month or the current posting year.
scr_ap_setting_a_system_action_when_a_tr.outcome: The company's budget discipline is enforced by the system at entry rather than discovered during month-end variance review.
scr_ap_setting_a_system_action_when_a_tr.rootCause: Budget overruns discovered at close are already sunk costs — the vendor has performed and the liability exists. Moving the control to the point of entry is the difference between a preventive and a detective control, and choosing Warn instead of Prevent quietly turns a preventive control into an advisory message that SOC 1 testers will not credit.
scr_ap_setting_a_system_action_when_a_tr.ifSkipped: Every budget breach becomes a post-facto variance explanation, and the owner's approved budget stops functioning as a spending limit.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, preventive versus detective control design
Loan agreement approved-budget covenants
Partnership agreement major-decision thresholds
redFlags: Warn selected everywhere so no transaction is ever blocked
Budget check duration set to Current year, masking monthly overruns
Check disabled for one property during a value-add program and never re-enabled
scr_ap_setting_a_system_action_when_a_tr.yardi: Yardi Voyager: budget validation on payables and POs configured per property in Setup, with Forecast IQ budgets as the comparison basis.

scr_ap_expense_report_approvals.purpose: Routes employee expense reports — mileage, site supplies bought on a personal card, travel between portfolio properties — through the same approval workflow as vendor invoices, subject to the Company application subscription and at least one financial application.
scr_ap_expense_report_approvals.outcome: Employee reimbursements carry the same documented approval as third-party invoices before they become a payable to the employee.
scr_ap_expense_report_approvals.rootCause: Reimbursements are the disbursement class most often approved informally, because the payee is a colleague and the amounts look small. They are also where personal expenses most often enter the property's operating statement, and an owner reading 6410 Administrative cannot see that a line was a manager's dinner rather than a property cost.
scr_ap_expense_report_approvals.ifSkipped: Personal spending is reimbursed against property expense accounts with no approval on file, creating both an owner chargeback and a taxable-fringe exposure.
gaap: IRC §62(c) — accountable plan requirements for non-taxable reimbursement
Treas. Reg. §1.62-2 — substantiation and return of excess
COSO 2013 — Principle 10, authorization of disbursements
redFlags: Expense reports approved by the submitter's direct report
Reimbursements without itemized receipts, failing the accountable plan test
Recurring personal-card purchases that should be on a property PO
scr_ap_expense_report_approvals.yardi: Yardi Voyager: no native expense-report module — reimbursements are entered as payables to an employee vendor and routed through PAYscan workflow.

scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.purpose: Explains that approve and decline actions are available only from the My Approvals view of the Approval workbench and not from View All, then walks through single and bulk approval plus the mandatory reason field on a decline.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.outcome: Approvers act only on items genuinely assigned to them, and every decline carries a written reason the submitter can act on.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.rootCause: The two-view design is a segregation-of-duties device: View All exists for visibility, My Approvals for authority, and an approver who cannot find the Approve link is usually looking at a transaction that is not theirs to approve. Forcing a typed reason on decline converts a rejection from a silent bounce into evidence that the control operated.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.ifSkipped: Transactions bounce back with no explanation, submitters resubmit unchanged, and the approval cycle adds days to the payment run without improving the invoice.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, segregation of duties in authorization
SOC 1 — evidence that the approval control operated
redFlags: Bulk approval of dozens of invoices in a single click without opening any
Declines carrying a one-character reason
Approvers working from View All and asking others to click Approve for them
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.yardi: Yardi Voyager: the 'My Approvals' inbox in PAYscan workflow; bulk approve from the invoice register with a required comment on rejection.

scr_ap_available_budget_page_2.purpose: Documents the Available budget page reached from the Spend control on an A/P invoice, purchase order or subcontract, and how its tab set changes with the transaction's line entry type — Month, Year to date and Current year for standard lines, job cost columns for job cost lines.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_2.outcome: Whoever opens the panel understands which budget basis they are reading, rather than assuming the first tab is the whole picture.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_2.rootCause: The same page means different things depending on how the transaction was coded. A reviewer looking at a job cost invoice expects a project-to-date budget and instead sees a monthly operating figure if the lines were entered as standard, which is how capital work gets approved against an operating budget line that was never meant to fund it.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_2.ifSkipped: Approvers read the wrong budget basis and clear capital spend against a monthly operating allowance, distorting both the operating statement and capex tracking.
gaap: ASC 360-10 — capitalization versus expense of property costs
COSO 2013 — Principle 13, quality information for decision-making
redFlags: Job work entered on standard lines so the job budget is never checked
Approvers deciding from the Month tab on annual contracts
Remaining figures that exclude unapproved invoices already queued

scr_ap_approval_configuration_page.purpose: The single company-level page where approval workflow is switched on or off for each transaction class — journal entries, A/P invoices, purchase orders, service contracts, subcontracts, job cost transactions and change orders, and A/P payments.
scr_ap_approval_configuration_page.outcome: A one-screen statement of which transaction types require approval at all, which is the first page an auditor asks to see.
scr_ap_approval_configuration_page.rootCause: Approval policies and workflows are elaborate, but they only run for transaction classes enabled here. A company can hold a thick policy matrix and still be disbursing cash without approval because the A/P payment checkbox on this page was never ticked — the policies exist but nothing routes to them.
scr_ap_approval_configuration_page.ifSkipped: Entire transaction classes post without any approval routing, and the documented control described in the SOC 1 narrative does not exist in the system.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, deployment of control activities through policy
SOC 1 — control design versus control operation
redFlags: Journal entry approval left disabled while the control narrative claims it operates
A/P payment approval off, so cash leaves without a second signature
Configuration changed mid-year with no change ticket
scr_ap_approval_configuration_page.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Administration > Workflow setup, where each transaction type is separately enabled for workflow routing.

scr_ap_configuring_transaction_approvals.purpose: Fills in each transaction-type section of the approval configuration — enabling journal entry approval, choosing whether declined transactions may be deleted, and selecting whose contact details appear on automatic vendor payment notification emails.
scr_ap_configuring_transaction_approvals.outcome: Each transaction class carries settings matched to how that class is actually controlled, saved as one configuration record.
scr_ap_configuring_transaction_approvals.rootCause: The 'Ability to delete declined approvals' option is the dangerous setting here: it overrides a system configuration that otherwise forbids deleting transactions. Turning it on lets a declined invoice vanish rather than sit in the queue as evidence that someone tried to push it through, which is precisely the evidence an investigator later needs.
scr_ap_configuring_transaction_approvals.ifSkipped: Settings default inconsistently across transaction classes, and declined items either pile up unworkable or disappear without trace depending on which checkbox was left as shipped.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, policy translated into system settings
SOC 1 — retention of evidence that a control operated
redFlags: Delete-declined enabled company-wide rather than for a documented exception
Payment notification contact pointing at a shared mailbox nobody reads
Journal entry approval enabled but with no policy behind it

scr_ap_defining_a_default_approver.purpose: Names the fallback approver who picks up a transaction when the workflow has a gap — the assigned role has no users, the only user in the role is inactive, nobody in the role has access to the transaction's entity, or an A/P payment method has no workflow for that location.
scr_ap_defining_a_default_approver.outcome: No transaction can stall in a broken routing path, because an identified person receives it and the submitter sees a warning that the gap occurred.
scr_ap_defining_a_default_approver.rootCause: Approval matrices decay quietly. A regional manager resigns, their role empties, and every invoice for their six properties routes to nobody — the queue simply does not advance and nobody is told. The default approver exists to make that failure visible and payable rather than invisible and stuck through a whole payment cycle.
scr_ap_defining_a_default_approver.ifSkipped: Invoices sit in limbo behind an empty role, vendors go unpaid past terms, and lien or late-fee exposure builds on properties with no one watching the queue.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 3, assignment of authority and responsibility
State prompt-payment statutes for construction trades
redFlags: Default approver set to a single controller who then approves everything by exception
Routing-gap warnings ignored by submitters
Roles left with zero active users for a full month

scr_ap_disabling_auto_approvals_for_tran.purpose: Turns off the automatic self-approval that otherwise occurs when the submitter sits at the first approval level, or when one person's approval under one role satisfies the same role in a second policy that also applies to the transaction.
scr_ap_disabling_auto_approvals_for_tran.outcome: A transaction requiring three approval levels genuinely collects three separate human decisions rather than collapsing into fewer.
scr_ap_disabling_auto_approvals_for_tran.rootCause: Auto-approval is a convenience feature that quietly destroys segregation of duties: a property manager who enters an invoice and also holds the Property Manager approval role has, by default, approved their own invoice. Where two policies both demand the Accounting Clerk role, the second requirement is satisfied by the same click — so a policy documented as requiring two clerks operates with one.
scr_ap_disabling_auto_approvals_for_tran.ifSkipped: Approval levels documented to auditors as independent collapse to a single signature, and the portfolio is running self-approved disbursements.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, segregation of incompatible duties
SOC 1 — approval control operating as designed
redFlags: Submitter and first-level approver being the same person on high-value invoices
Multi-policy overlap collapsing a two-clerk requirement to one
Auto-approve left enabled on A/P payments
scr_ap_disabling_auto_approvals_for_tran.yardi: Yardi Voyager: workflow setup can exclude the submitter from their own approval step; overlapping role approvals are configured per workflow.

scr_ap_automatically_advancing_a_p_invoi.purpose: Enables a time-based escalation on A/P invoice and purchase order approvals so that after a configured number of days without action the item moves to the next approver in the chain, illustrated by a three-level route where one person holds roles at two levels.
scr_ap_automatically_advancing_a_p_invoi.outcome: Approval queues keep moving through vacations and turnover without anyone manually reassigning items.
scr_ap_automatically_advancing_a_p_invoi.rootCause: Escalation solves an aging problem but creates an authority problem: the level that timed out never actually reviewed the invoice, so the control owner delegation depends on was skipped even though the audit trail shows the item as approved. The day threshold must be long enough that escalation stays genuinely exceptional rather than becoming the normal path to payment.
scr_ap_automatically_advancing_a_p_invoi.ifSkipped: Invoices age in one approver's queue past vendor terms, early-pay discounts lapse, and trades on capital projects start filing preliminary lien notices.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, delegated authority limits
State mechanic's lien and prompt-payment statutes
redFlags: Threshold set to one or two days so escalation becomes the default route
A high proportion of approvals recorded as auto-advanced
Escalation enabled on capital change orders that need a named signature

scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_list.purpose: The central register of approval policies, which RealPage matches against each new transaction's attributes — amount, vendor, GL account, job type — to decide who must approve it, across journal entries, A/P invoices, POs, service contracts, subcontracts, job cost change orders, A/P payments and PO change orders.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_list.outcome: One list showing every rule that can route a transaction, ready to be exported and reconciled against the owner's delegation-of-authority schedule.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_list.rootCause: Delegation of authority in a management agreement is written as a table of dollar limits by role; this list is the system's version of that table. Where the two disagree — a policy limit set higher than the management agreement allows — the manager is committing the owner beyond its authority on every transaction that matches.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_list.ifSkipped: Nobody can demonstrate what the approval rules are, and the delegation schedule in the management agreement goes untested against the system that is supposed to enforce it.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 3, authority and responsibility
Management agreement delegation-of-authority limits
SOC 1 — control design documentation
redFlags: Policy limits exceeding the management agreement's delegated thresholds
Overlapping policies whose combined effect nobody has traced
Policies with no active users in the assigned role
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_list.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Administration > Workflow setup lists approval rules by transaction type, amount band and property.

scr_ap_adding_approval_policies.purpose: Creates a new approval policy — choosing a policy type such as Amount, Tiered amount, Vendor, GL account or Job type, naming it, and assigning the role or user who approves the transactions the policy captures.
scr_ap_adding_approval_policies.outcome: A new, named routing rule exists and begins matching transactions the next time one is entered.
scr_ap_adding_approval_policies.rootCause: The policy type chosen at creation fixes what the rule can ever test, and the policy name cannot be edited afterwards. Choosing Amount when the real control is by GL account means capital work under the threshold escapes the capital approver entirely, and the fix is a second policy rather than an edit — which is how portfolios accumulate overlapping rules nobody can reason about.
scr_ap_adding_approval_policies.ifSkipped: Spend categories the owner expected to be controlled — capital accounts, related-party vendors, specific job types — route on amount alone and reach payment without the right reviewer.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, policies and procedures deployed
ASC 850 — related party transactions requiring elevated approval
redFlags: Amount-only policies on a portfolio running capital programs
Related-party vendors with no dedicated policy
Policy names that do not describe what the policy does

scr_ap_viewing_or_editing_an_approval_po.purpose: Opens an existing policy in View mode — where it can be printed, exported as XML, duplicated and its audit trail inspected — or in Edit mode, which additionally allows the approval routing, limits and status to be changed.
scr_ap_viewing_or_editing_an_approval_po.outcome: A reviewer can read and evidence a policy without holding rights to change it, and changes that are made leave an audit trail on the policy record.
scr_ap_viewing_or_editing_an_approval_po.rootCause: The View/Edit split is what lets internal audit examine the control without becoming part of it. The policy's own audit trail matters more than the policy text: a SOC 1 tester needs to know whether a limit was $5,000 on the date the disputed invoice was approved, not what it says today.
scr_ap_viewing_or_editing_an_approval_po.ifSkipped: Reviewers are given edit rights just to read policies, and nobody can prove what a limit was on a historical approval date.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 11, access rights matched to responsibilities
SOC 1 — change management over control configuration
redFlags: Auditors granted Edit rather than View access
Policy audit trail showing limit changes with no change ticket
Limits raised shortly before a large transaction was approved

scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_page.purpose: The two-section policy editor itself: an upper section fixing the policy's primary attributes (type, name, status) and a lower Approval routing and limits section defining who approves and up to what amount.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_page.outcome: Policy identity and policy routing are captured in one record, so the rule and its dollar limits travel together.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_page.rootCause: Separating identity from routing on the same page is what makes a limit meaningful — a policy called 'Regional Manager approval' with routing that stops at $250,000 is a different control from the same name capped at $10,000. Reviewers who read only the policy list see the name and assume the limit, which is why the page shows both together.
scr_ap_approval_policy_manager_page.ifSkipped: Policies are judged by their names rather than their limits, and a routing row with an unintended ceiling passes review unnoticed.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 3, delegated authority defined in writing
Management agreement delegation-of-authority limits
redFlags: Routing limits left at an unbounded default
Policy name and actual limit telling different stories
Inactive policies still matching transactions because status was never updated

scr_ap_adding_another_approval_routing_a.purpose: Adds a further routing row to a policy — selecting another user or role and setting Require approvers from one to four, with the caution not to require more approvers than the role has active users.
scr_ap_adding_another_approval_routing_a.outcome: A policy can demand several independent sign-offs at one level, and the count is set against a role that can actually supply them.
scr_ap_adding_another_approval_routing_a.rootCause: Requiring three approvers from a role with two active users creates a queue nothing can ever clear — the transaction is permanently one approval short and only a configuration change releases it. This is the most common way a well-intentioned tightening of controls freezes a property's payment cycle for a full week.
scr_ap_adding_another_approval_routing_a.ifSkipped: Either the multi-signature requirement the owner asked for is never built, or it is built against an understaffed role and deadlocks the queue.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, multiple-approval control design
SOC 1 — controls capable of operating as designed
redFlags: Require approvers set above the count of active users in the role
Routing rows added without removing the superseded row
Four-approver requirements imposed on routine low-value invoices

scr_ap_changing_an_approver_of_a_transac.purpose: Swaps the role or user in a policy's Approval routing and limits row for a different one, noting that a person missing from the drop-down first needs transaction approval workflow permissions granted.
scr_ap_changing_an_approver_of_a_transac.outcome: Approval authority follows the current org chart rather than the one in place when the policy was written.
scr_ap_changing_an_approver_of_a_transac.rootCause: Approver changes are usually made under pressure — someone has left, the queue is backing up — and the change takes effect immediately for every transaction the policy matches, with no notice to anyone who relied on the old routing. That is exactly the moment to check whether the incoming approver's limit matches what the management agreement delegates to their position.
scr_ap_changing_an_approver_of_a_transac.ifSkipped: Departed employees remain named approvers, their accounts stay active so the queue keeps moving, and terminated users hold live approval authority over cash.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 4, competence and timely access changes
SOC 1 — user access termination controls
redFlags: Terminated users still named in active policies
Approver swapped to a junior role to clear a backlog
Permissions granted solely to make someone appear in the drop-down

scr_ap_auto_approving_transaction_amount.purpose: Explains the built-in behaviour of Amount and Tiered amount policies whereby RealPage auto-approves every level at or below the submitter's own approval authority — so a CFO entering a transaction does not wait on a property manager or regional manager beneath them.
scr_ap_auto_approving_transaction_amount.outcome: Senior submitters are not routed through subordinates for approvals they already outrank, and the transaction advances to the first level genuinely above them.
scr_ap_auto_approving_transaction_amount.rootCause: This shortcut is defensible when the submitter's own limit covers the amount, and indefensible when it is the only approval the transaction ever receives. A CFO entering a $400,000 subcontract clears their own levels and, if no higher level exists in the policy, has self-approved a commitment — the classic override-of-controls scenario auditors test for at the top of the house.
scr_ap_auto_approving_transaction_amount.ifSkipped: Either senior staff waste cycles waiting on subordinates, or — with the behaviour left unexamined — senior transactions reach payment on a single self-generated approval.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 1, management override of controls
AU-C 240 — risk of management override in fraud consideration
SOC 1 — tone at the top and control environment
redFlags: Senior-submitted transactions with no approver other than the submitter
Tiered policies with no level above the executive tier
A rise in high-value transactions entered directly by officers

scr_ap_inactivating_an_approval_policy.purpose: Retires an approval policy by setting its Status to Inactive rather than deleting it, so historical transactions still reference the rule that routed them while new transactions stop matching it.
scr_ap_inactivating_an_approval_policy.outcome: The policy stops routing immediately, and the approvals already granted under it remain traceable to the rule that was in force.
scr_ap_inactivating_an_approval_policy.rootCause: Deleting a policy would orphan the approval history of every transaction it ever routed, leaving an auditor with an approval record that names a policy no longer in the system. Inactivation preserves that link, which matters because the audit question is never what the rules are now, but what they were on the date the disbursement was authorised.
scr_ap_inactivating_an_approval_policy.ifSkipped: Transactions keep routing to a rule the company believes is retired, or — if deleted instead — the approval history loses the policy reference an auditor needs to test authorisation.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, retiring superseded control activities
SOC 1 — audit evidence retention over the review period
redFlags: Policies deleted rather than inactivated
A policy inactivated with no replacement, silently removing an approval level
Inactivation dates that do not match the change ticket

scr_ap_spend_policy_manager.purpose: Sets up spend policies that tie spending rules to specific GL account ranges — a from and to account, a role or user, a policy name and status — so a category of spend such as capital accounts or utilities can be governed separately from dollar-amount routing.
scr_ap_spend_policy_manager.outcome: Spend rules exist by GL account range and can be referenced while viewing, editing or reviewing a transaction.
scr_ap_spend_policy_manager.rootCause: Dollar thresholds alone cannot distinguish a $40,000 roof replacement from $40,000 of turnover painting, yet one belongs in 1530 Building Improvements under the asset manager's eye and the other in 6110 Repairs & Maintenance under the regional manager's. Account-range policies are how capital-versus-expense judgement gets a named reviewer instead of being decided by whoever coded the invoice.
scr_ap_spend_policy_manager.ifSkipped: Capital and operating spend are routed identically on amount alone, and the ASC 360 capitalisation decision is made by a coder with no reviewer.
gaap: ASC 360-10-30 — capitalisation of costs that better or restore a unit of property
Treas. Reg. §1.263(a)-3 — tangible property regulations
COSO 2013 — Principle 12, policies deployed by spend category
redFlags: GL ranges that leave gaps so some accounts match no spend policy
Capital account ranges routed to an operating approver
Ranges written against an old chart of accounts after a remap

scr_ap_editing_a_spend_policy.purpose: Edits an existing spend policy's fields — role or user, GL account from and to, status — with the policy name locked because other records reference it.
scr_ap_editing_a_spend_policy.outcome: The spend rule is corrected in place, keeping its name and the history attached to it.
scr_ap_editing_a_spend_policy.rootCause: Widening a GL account range is the change with the longest reach: extending a range from 6110 through 6210 to cover the whole 6000 series silently pulls management fees and real estate taxes under an approver who was only ever meant to see maintenance spend. Nothing on the edit screen shows how many accounts the change captures.
scr_ap_editing_a_spend_policy.ifSkipped: Spend policies drift out of alignment with the chart of accounts, so newly added GL accounts fall outside every range and route with no category-based review.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, keeping policies current with the chart of accounts
SOC 1 — change management over control parameters
redFlags: Account ranges widened without listing the accounts newly captured
Edits made without a change ticket
New GL accounts added with no corresponding spend policy update

scr_ap_duplicating_a_spend_policy.purpose: Creates a new spend policy from an existing one, copying the Approval routing and limits section while leaving the Policy name blank, so a proven rule can be adapted to a new account range or entity.
scr_ap_duplicating_a_spend_policy.outcome: A second policy built from a known-good template, needing only a name, a status and any range changes.
scr_ap_duplicating_a_spend_policy.rootCause: Duplication is fast and that is the risk: the routing carries over intact, so a policy copied from one owner's entity keeps that owner's approvers unless someone remembers to change them. In a multi-owner portfolio that means one institutional owner's regional manager silently holding approval authority over another owner's property.
scr_ap_duplicating_a_spend_policy.ifSkipped: Each new policy is rebuilt by hand, routing is inconsistent across otherwise identical entities, and the variation shows up as unexplained approval differences in audit testing.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, consistent deployment across entities
ASC 810 — separate governance of consolidated entities
ASC 850 — related party authority boundaries
redFlags: Copied policies retaining the source entity's approvers
Duplicates left Inactive and forgotten
Near-identical policy names that reviewers cannot tell apart

scr_ap_approval_workflow_list.purpose: Lists approval workflows, each of which binds a set of approval policies to specific properties, with a Flipview toggle that re-lists the same data by property so gaps in coverage become visible.
scr_ap_approval_workflow_list.outcome: Every property can be checked against the workflow governing it, from either direction.
scr_ap_approval_workflow_list.rootCause: Policies define who approves; workflows define where those policies apply. A newly acquired property that is not attached to any workflow inherits only the auto-generated default, so its invoices route to the default approver and nobody notices until the first payment cycle. The Flipview by property is the fastest way to find that property.
scr_ap_approval_workflow_list.ifSkipped: Properties acquired mid-year operate outside the intended approval structure, and their disbursements carry an approval trail that does not match the owner's agreement.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, controls deployed across all in-scope entities
SOC 1 — completeness of the control population
redFlags: Properties appearing under no workflow in Flipview
Auto-generated default workflows never replaced after go-live
Disposed properties still attached to active workflows

scr_ap_adding_a_new_policy_to_an_approva.purpose: Attaches an additional policy to an existing workflow through the Workflow wizard, selecting it in the next blank Policy name row and optionally flagging it as an Override.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_policy_to_an_approva.outcome: The workflow now evaluates one more rule for the properties it covers, with override behaviour explicitly chosen.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_policy_to_an_approva.rootCause: The Override checkbox is the consequential field: an override policy supersedes the others rather than adding to them, so ticking it can remove approval levels the workflow was built to enforce. It is ticked most often to fast-track an urgent vendor and then left on, quietly weakening the routing for every subsequent transaction the policy matches.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_policy_to_an_approva.ifSkipped: New spend categories or elevated approvers are never wired into the workflow, so the policy exists in the manager list but never fires on a real transaction.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, control activity design and override risk
SOC 1 — evidence of configuration changes
redFlags: Override ticked on a policy that should have been additive
Policies added to a workflow with no test transaction run afterwards
Temporary override policies still active months later

scr_ap_viewing_and_editing_approval_work.purpose: Opens a workflow in the Workflow wizard from the list's View or Edit link, to read or change its policy set, property assignments and conditions before saving or returning with Done.
scr_ap_viewing_and_editing_approval_work.outcome: The workflow's current composition can be inspected and adjusted as an entity's structure changes.
scr_ap_viewing_and_editing_approval_work.rootCause: Workflows are edited when portfolios move — properties transfer between managers, an owner sells half a fund, a new regional structure is announced. The property assignment inside the workflow is the piece that actually determines whose invoices route where, and it is the piece that lags behind the org announcement by weeks.
scr_ap_viewing_and_editing_approval_work.ifSkipped: Workflows keep routing to the previous management structure, and approvals are granted by people no longer responsible for those properties.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 3, structures and reporting lines kept current
ASC 810 — entity-level governance boundaries
redFlags: Property assignments not updated after a portfolio transfer
Workflow edits saved with Done before Save
Conditions left enabled from a prior structure

scr_ap_deleting_an_approval_workflow.purpose: Removes an approval workflow entirely after a confirmation prompt, unbinding the policies it held from the properties it covered.
scr_ap_deleting_an_approval_workflow.outcome: The workflow no longer exists, and its properties fall back to whatever other workflow or default approver covers them.
scr_ap_deleting_an_approval_workflow.rootCause: Deletion is instantaneous and unconfirmed beyond a single OK, and it does not tell you which properties were attached. Those properties do not stop transacting — they simply route through the default approver from the next invoice onward, which looks like a working control right up until an auditor asks who approved a $60,000 roof and the answer is the system's fallback.
scr_ap_deleting_an_approval_workflow.ifSkipped: Obsolete workflows keep matching transactions and routing them to approvers who no longer hold the properties, producing approvals nobody intended to grant.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 12, controlled retirement of control activities
SOC 1 — evidence retention for the review period
redFlags: Workflow deleted without first listing its properties
No replacement workflow created before deletion
Deletions with no change ticket during an audit period

scr_ap_defining_approval_workflow_condit.purpose: Builds the gate that decides whether a workflow applies at all — a conditions list combined with All (AND), Any (OR), or a written expression such as (1 AND 2) OR (2 AND 3) that references the condition row numbers.
scr_ap_defining_approval_workflow_condit.outcome: The workflow's policies are evaluated only for transactions matching the stated criteria, and skipped entirely for the rest.
scr_ap_defining_approval_workflow_condit.rootCause: Conditions are evaluated before policies, so a mistake here does not misroute a transaction — it exempts it from approval altogether. An expression written with row numbers is especially brittle: inserting a condition renumbers the rows, and an expression that read correctly yesterday can silently start excluding the transactions it was written to capture.
scr_ap_defining_approval_workflow_condit.ifSkipped: Either every transaction is forced through a heavyweight workflow regardless of size, or a badly written expression lets a whole class of spend bypass approval unnoticed.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, completeness of control coverage
SOC 1 — testing that controls apply to the full population
redFlags: Expressions referencing row numbers that changed after a condition was inserted
Conditions never tested against a sample of real transactions
Transactions found posted with no approval record at all

scr_ap_submitter_conditions_in_approval_.purpose: Uses Submitter or Submitter role as the condition policy type, so a workflow fires only when a named individual or role enters a transaction — or fires for everyone except them.
scr_ap_submitter_conditions_in_approval_.outcome: Approval routing can be tightened around a specific person or role, or deliberately relaxed for one, with the rule written down rather than informally understood.
scr_ap_submitter_conditions_in_approval_.rootCause: Submitter conditions are the mechanism behind both the best and the worst control in the module. Used to force extra approval on transactions entered by an officer, they are a genuine anti-override control; used in the negative form to exempt that same officer, they create a documented, system-enforced bypass that nobody outside system administration will ever see.
scr_ap_submitter_conditions_in_approval_.ifSkipped: Everyone's transactions route identically, so a president or CFO entering a payment gets the same routine review as a leasing consultant's supply order.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 1, integrity and management override
AU-C 240 — journal entries and transactions outside normal course
ASC 850 — related party transaction scrutiny
redFlags: Negative submitter conditions exempting named executives
Submitter conditions added with no documented business reason
Conditions naming individuals rather than roles, surviving their departure

scr_ap_approval_workbench_2.purpose: The Approval workbench itself — a filters panel above a transaction list where pending items can be approved, closed, declined, viewed or edited, with options to add another approver or export the queue to Excel.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_2.outcome: Every transaction awaiting a decision anywhere in the company is visible on one page, with the actions available on each.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_2.rootCause: Before a single queue existed, approvals lived in email threads and nobody could say how much unapproved spend the portfolio was carrying. The workbench turns that into a measurable number, which matters at close because unapproved invoices sitting in the queue are still liabilities that belong in the accrual if the goods were received before period end.
scr_ap_approval_workbench_2.ifSkipped: Pending spend is invisible, month-end accruals miss received-but-unapproved invoices, and 2020 Accrued Expenses understates the property's true obligations.
gaap: ASC 405-10 — recognition of liabilities regardless of approval status
COSO 2013 — Principle 10, centralised authorisation
IRC §461(h) — economic performance for accrual deduction
redFlags: Large unapproved balances at period end with no accrual booked
Items in the queue older than the vendor's payment terms
Workbench exports circulated without a cut-off date
scr_ap_approval_workbench_2.yardi: Yardi Voyager: PAYscan invoice register / workflow queue, with 'My Approvals' and portfolio-wide views.

scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_workbench_2.purpose: Covers how requesters, not just approvers, open the workbench with the right permissions to track the status of transactions they submitted, switching between the View all and My approvals perspectives and selecting a transaction type.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_workbench_2.outcome: A submitter can see where their own invoice or PO is sitting without emailing the approver to ask.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_workbench_2.rootCause: Most approval delays are really status-visibility problems: the submitter assumes the item is moving, the approver never saw the notification, and the vendor calls a fortnight later. Giving requesters read access to the queue converts a chase-by-email culture into one where the person who cares most about the item is also the one monitoring it.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_workbench_2.ifSkipped: Submitters chase approvers by phone and email, approval aging goes unmanaged, and the A/P team absorbs the vendor's calls about an invoice nobody is actually working.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 14, internal communication of control status
State prompt-payment statutes for trade contractors
redFlags: Requesters denied view rights and chasing by email instead
Submitters given approve rights when only view was needed
Status questions routed to A/P rather than the named approver

scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.purpose: Narrows the queue by transaction type and then by the type-specific criteria that appear — vendor, property, date, job — with filter selections retained across transaction-type switches until Clear is pressed.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.outcome: An approver works a manageable subset, such as one property's invoices, instead of scrolling the entire company queue.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.rootCause: Retained filters are the trap. A regional manager filters to one property on Monday, switches transaction type on Thursday, and the property filter is still applied — so the queue looks empty and eleven invoices for the other five properties are never seen. The filter that improves focus is the same filter that hides work.
scr_ap_filtering_transactions_in_the_app.ifSkipped: Approvers scroll an undifferentiated company-wide list, miss items for their own properties, and approval aging climbs on the properties furthest down the sort.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 13, complete and relevant information for decisions
SOC 1 — completeness of the queue reviewed
redFlags: A sticky property or vendor filter hiding items from the approver
Queues that look empty while the Aging report shows pending items
Filters saved as default without the owner realising

scr_ap_using_the_approval_workbench.purpose: Covers the list-shaping tools on the workbench — dragging a field into Row groups to group change orders by property, submission date or submitter, plus showing, hiding, reordering, resizing and searching columns.
scr_ap_using_the_approval_workbench.outcome: The queue is arranged so related items are reviewed together rather than approved one at a time out of context.
scr_ap_using_the_approval_workbench.rootCause: Grouping by submitter is the control use of this screen, not a cosmetic one: three change orders from the same person on the same job, each just under the approval threshold, look innocuous in date order and obviously structured when grouped. Hiding a column has the opposite effect — an approver who has hidden Amount or Property is approving on vendor name alone.
scr_ap_using_the_approval_workbench.ifSkipped: Related change orders are approved individually with no view of their cumulative effect, and split transactions designed to stay under a limit pass unchallenged.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 8, assessing fraud risk including transaction splitting
ASC 360-10 — cumulative capitalised project costs
redFlags: Amount or Property columns hidden from the approver's view
Multiple change orders from one submitter each sitting just under a limit
Grouping never used on jobs with heavy change order activity

scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.purpose: The Approval workbench approve and decline procedure as reached from the Company > All > Approvals path, including the Review & approve fast path for working through A/P invoices back to back and the bulk selection option.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.outcome: Batches of pending items are cleared with each decision recorded against the approver's name, comment and timestamp.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.rootCause: Speed is the point of this screen and the risk in it. An approver clearing forty invoices in nine minutes has, arithmetically, spent thirteen seconds per invoice — and thirteen seconds is not enough to open the attachment, check the property and confirm the coding. That pattern is visible in the timestamps on the Approval History Audit Report, and it is what a SOC 1 tester samples for.
scr_ap_approving_and_declining_transacti.ifSkipped: Items sit unactioned past terms, or are cleared so fast the approval is a keystroke rather than a review and provides no real assurance over the disbursement.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, control activities performed with due care
SOC 1 — operating effectiveness, not just existence, of approval
redFlags: Approval timestamps seconds apart across dozens of invoices
Bulk approvals covering multiple properties and vendors in one action
Approvals recorded outside business hours in clusters

scr_ap_reviewing_and_approving_a_p_invoi.purpose: The Review & approve button that appears once the workbench is filtered to A/P invoices, opening each invoice in queue order with its attachment displayed — and, for eInvoices, pushing the approved status back to OpsMerchant so the vendor sees it move from Pending to Approved.
scr_ap_reviewing_and_approving_a_p_invoi.outcome: Invoices are approved with the scanned document on screen, and eInvoice vendors are told the outcome without anyone emailing them.
scr_ap_reviewing_and_approving_a_p_invoi.rootCause: Approving from a list row means approving a vendor name and a number; approving from this screen means approving against the actual invoice image. The difference shows up in duplicate detection and in coding — a scanned invoice that says 'roof replacement, Building C' will not be approved into 6110 Repairs & Maintenance by an approver who is looking at it.
scr_ap_reviewing_and_approving_a_p_invoi.ifSkipped: Approvals are granted against list rows rather than documents, so capital work is cleared into repairs expense and duplicate vendor invoices pass a second time.
gaap: ASC 360-10-30 — capital versus expense determination on review
Treas. Reg. §1.263(a)-3 — tangible property regulations
COSO 2013 — Principle 10, approval supported by source documentation
redFlags: Invoices approved with no attachment on file
eInvoice statuses stuck at Pending after posting
Image viewer disabled so approvers never see the document
scr_ap_reviewing_and_approving_a_p_invoi.yardi: Yardi Voyager: PAYscan invoice approval with the scanned image displayed beside the coding grid; VendorCafe reflects the status back to the vendor.

scr_ap_saving_a_custom_workbench_view.purpose: Saves a set of workbench filters, transaction type and column selections as a named view — for example 'A/P invoices for Alpha Properties' — optionally marking it the default loaded every time the workbench opens.
scr_ap_saving_a_custom_workbench_view.outcome: Recurring review routines load in one click instead of being rebuilt each session.
scr_ap_saving_a_custom_workbench_view.rootCause: A default view is a standing decision about what the approver sees, taken once and never revisited. A saved view that excludes on-hold invoices, or one property, or declined items, becomes invisible after the first week — the approver stops experiencing it as a filter and starts experiencing it as the complete queue, which is how a property goes three cycles without anyone approving anything.
scr_ap_saving_a_custom_workbench_view.ifSkipped: Approvers rebuild the same filters daily, apply them inconsistently, and the queue each person reviews differs from the queue anyone else would see.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 13, completeness of information used in the control
SOC 1 — population completeness in control performance
redFlags: Default views that silently exclude a property or transaction type
Saved views never reconciled against the Aging report total
Views built by one person and inherited by their successor unexamined

scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.purpose: Lets a current approver insert an additional approver into a specific transaction's route, choosing from users who already hold access to the transaction's location and recording a comment explaining why.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.outcome: One transaction picks up an extra reviewer — an asset manager, a construction lead — without the policy being changed for everything else.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.rootCause: This is the escape valve for judgement that a policy cannot encode: a $9,800 invoice technically inside a limit but for work the regional manager wants the owner's asset manager to see. Adding rather than deferring keeps the item moving and leaves the reason on the audit trail, so the added step reads as deliberate rather than as a queue anomaly.
scr_ap_adding_an_approver_to_a_transacti.ifSkipped: Approvers either rubber-stamp items they are uneasy about or decline them outright, forcing re-entry and adding a full cycle to an invoice that only needed a second opinion.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 10, judgement applied within the control framework
ASC 850 — additional scrutiny of related party transactions
redFlags: Approvers added with a blank comment
The same approver repeatedly added, indicating the policy itself is wrong
Extra approvers added to spread accountability rather than to obtain review

scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.purpose: Returns a transaction to whoever approved it at the prior level — singly or in bulk from My approvals — with a comment, rather than declining it outright and sending it back to the submitter.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.outcome: A questionable item goes back one step to the person who cleared it, and leaves the current approver's queue.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.rootCause: Send back preserves the chain of accountability that a decline destroys. Declining wipes the route and returns the invoice to the submitter, who re-enters it and may well route it to a different first-level approver; sending back puts the question to the specific person who approved it, on the record, which is the only way a later reviewer can see that a lower-level approval was actually challenged.
scr_ap_sending_a_transaction_back_to_the.ifSkipped: Reviewers decline items rather than questioning the prior approval, the approval chain restarts, and the pattern of one approver's work being repeatedly queried never becomes visible.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 16, evaluation of whether controls operate effectively
SOC 1 — evidence of supervisory review
redFlags: Send-backs concentrated on one approver with no follow-up
Bulk send-backs with a generic comment
Items ping-ponging between two levels for weeks

scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.purpose: Opens the document attached to a queued transaction from the Actions column — the scanned vendor invoice, signed contract, lien waiver or delivery ticket — before the approver commits to a decision.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.outcome: The approver reads the supporting document rather than inferring the transaction from its header fields.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.rootCause: On construction and subcontract payments the attachment is not background reading, it is the control: the conditional or unconditional lien waiver for the prior payment must be on file before this one is released, or the owner pays the general contractor and remains exposed to a subcontractor's mechanic's lien on the same work. No field on the transaction header tells the approver whether that waiver is there.
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.ifSkipped: Payments are released without lien waivers, certificates of insurance or signed change orders, and the owner pays twice for work already funded once.
gaap: State mechanic's lien statutes and conditional/unconditional waiver requirements
COSO 2013 — Principle 10, approval supported by evidence
ASC 450 — contingencies arising from unresolved lien claims
redFlags: Pay applications approved with no lien waiver attached
Attachments that are unsigned drafts rather than executed documents
Certificates of insurance expired at the approval date
scr_ap_viewing_an_attachment_for_a_trans.yardi: Yardi Voyager: Document Management attachments on the payable, with lien waiver tracking in Construction Manager / Job Cost compliance.

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.purpose: Opens the Available budget page for a queued item by clicking the $ link in the workbench Actions column, showing budget and activity for the property and GL account carried on that transaction.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.outcome: The approver decides with the remaining budget for that exact account and property in front of them.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.rootCause: The approver is the last person who can stop an overspend, and unlike the submitter they usually have no independent knowledge of where the property sits against budget. Putting the check one click from the Approve link is what makes budget discipline a condition of approval rather than a variance conversation held six weeks later with the regional manager.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_for_.ifSkipped: Approvals are granted on the reasonableness of the invoice alone, and the first anyone hears of the overrun is the owner's variance question on the monthly package.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 13, relevant information available at the point of control
Loan agreement approved-budget covenants
redFlags: Approvals on over-budget lines with no written justification
The $ link never used on high-value items
Budget shown against an unpublished or superseded budget version

scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.purpose: Opens the Approval history box for one transaction by clicking its Status link in the workbench, listing each approver, action, date and comment for that item — with View all first if the transaction is outside the user's own queue.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.outcome: The full approval chain for a single transaction is readable on demand, without running a report.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.rootCause: When a vendor disputes a payment or an owner queries a charge, the question is always about one transaction and always asked months later. This box answers it in seconds and is the evidence exported into the month-end work papers, which is why the practical control point is remembering to export it — the on-screen view is transient and the underlying detail is not something the accountant controls the retention of.
scr_ap_viewing_the_approval_history_of_a.ifSkipped: Approval evidence for disputed items has to be reconstructed from the audit report under time pressure, and the specific chain may no longer be retrievable in the same form.
gaap: SOC 1 — evidence that the approval control operated on a sampled item
COSO 2013 — Principle 16, evaluating controls through their trail
AU-C 500 — sufficiency and appropriateness of audit evidence
redFlags: Approval history viewed but never exported into the work papers
Chains showing a single approver on amounts above the delegated limit
Comments that record no substantive reason for the decision

scr_ap_including_declined_transactions_i.purpose: Adds declined items to the workbench through the Include declined checkbox — they are excluded by default — so they can be edited and resubmitted, with the option to make that the default by saving a custom view.
scr_ap_including_declined_transactions_i.outcome: Declined transactions are visible and workable instead of sitting outside the queue everyone looks at.
scr_ap_including_declined_transactions_i.rootCause: Hiding declines by default is sensible for an approver and dangerous for the A/P team: a declined invoice is still an unpaid obligation with an aging vendor behind it, and it appears nowhere in the queue anyone monitors. The invoice is not gone, it is simply unwatched, and the next contact is usually the vendor threatening to stop service or file a lien.
scr_ap_including_declined_transactions_i.ifSkipped: Declined invoices disappear from view, are never corrected and resubmitted, and vendors on operating contracts stop work over a payable nobody knows is outstanding.
gaap: ASC 405-10 — a declined invoice remains a liability if the obligation exists
COSO 2013 — Principle 16, monitoring of exception items
State prompt-payment statutes
redFlags: Declined items older than thirty days with no resubmission
Declines never reviewed by anyone after the decline
Liabilities for declined-but-received goods missing from the accrual

scr_ap_approval_aging_report.purpose: Reports pending approvals by how long they have been waiting, broken out by vendor, transaction type, job and location, with drill-through from the Current state column into the approval history and from Amount into the transaction.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report.outcome: A measured view of where the approval process is slow, by approver and by property, rather than an impression of it.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report.rootCause: Approval aging is the leading indicator that A/P aging only confirms a month later. A vendor whose invoices consistently sit fourteen days in approval will show up as a late-payment problem, a lost early-pay discount and eventually a service interruption — but only the aging report identifies the specific approver and property where the delay originates while it is still fixable.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report.ifSkipped: Approval bottlenecks are diagnosed only after vendors escalate, discounts lapse and trade contractors begin filing preliminary lien notices.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 16, ongoing monitoring of control timeliness
State mechanic's lien notice deadlines
ASC 405-10 — completeness of recorded liabilities
redFlags: Items aged beyond the vendor's net terms
One approver holding a disproportionate share of the aged balance
Aged capital items on jobs with lien notice deadlines approaching
scr_ap_approval_aging_report.yardi: Yardi Voyager: PAYscan workflow aging / pending approval reports in Payable Analytics.

scr_ap_approval_aging_report_options.purpose: The setup page for the Approval Aging Report — running it straight on defaults with View, or using Customize to set the time period, Today versus a selected date, and the other filters before generating.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_options.outcome: The report is produced for a defined as-of point rather than whatever the default happened to be.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_options.rootCause: An aging report is meaningless without a stated as-of date, and this is where that date is set. Two people running it on defaults on different days produce different day-bucket counts for the same invoice, so an approval aging metric quoted in a management meeting has to carry its as-of date or it cannot be compared with last month's.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_options.ifSkipped: Aging figures circulate without an as-of date, period-over-period comparisons are invalid, and nobody can tell whether the backlog actually improved.
gaap: COSO 2013 — Principle 13, reliable and comparable information
SOC 1 — reproducibility of reports used as control evidence
redFlags: Reports circulated with no as-of date printed
Different as-of conventions used month to month
Prompt-on-run left off, so a memorised report silently uses a stale period

scr_ap_approval_aging_report_columns.purpose: Defines what each Approval Aging Report column means — vendor, order number, PO created date, employee and expense report name for reimbursements, date filed, and Current state as Submitted, Declined or Partially approved.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_columns.outcome: A reader interprets the report correctly rather than guessing what Partially approved implies about the item.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_columns.rootCause: Partially approved is the column value that misleads: it means some required approvers have signed and others have not, so the transaction is entirely unreleased and the property owes the full amount. Readers who treat it as nearly done under-accrue at period end and under-forecast the cash the check run will need.
scr_ap_approval_aging_report_columns.ifSkipped: Aging output is misread, partially approved items are treated as effectively cleared, and both the accrual and the cash forecast understate the obligation.

COSO 2013 — Principle 13, information that is understandable to its users

scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report.purpose: The report that evidences the approval control across transaction types — A/P invoices, purchase orders, service contracts, subcontracts, payments and expense reports — filterable by transaction number, status, vendor or location, and used to verify that approvals actually complied with the policies.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report.outcome: A defensible, filterable record that the company's approval policies were followed, produced for auditors rather than assembled by hand.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report.rootCause: This is the single deliverable a SOC 1 or financial statement auditor uses to test the authorisation control, and its value lies in the comparison it enables: not just that somebody approved each item, but that the approver named matches the policy that governed it. An invoice approved by a person whose limit was below the amount is an exception the report surfaces and no other screen will.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report.ifSkipped: The approval control can be described but not proven, and the auditor's alternative is a large sample of manual invoice inspection — or a control exception and expanded testing.
gaap: SOC 1 — operating effectiveness of the authorisation control
COSO 2013 — Principle 16, separate evaluations of control performance
AU-C 330 — tests of controls over disbursements
redFlags: Approvers named on amounts above their policy limit
Transactions posted with no approval row at all
Report never run outside the annual audit request
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report.yardi: Yardi Voyager: workflow history reporting from PAYscan plus Administration > User Activity / Change Log for the underlying audit trail.

scr_ap_customizing_and_running_the_appro.purpose: Runs the Approval History Audit report to a chosen reporting period and As of date, with Prompt on run to be asked at each execution, and up to 80 characters each of report title, subtitle and footer that appear only on the PDF produced by Print.
scr_ap_customizing_and_running_the_appro.outcome: A dated, titled PDF that identifies the period and the entity it covers, suitable for handing to an auditor.
scr_ap_customizing_and_running_the_appro.rootCause: An untitled PDF of approval history is worthless as an audit deliverable a year later — nobody can tell which entity, period or filter produced it. The title and footer fields are the only place that context is recorded on the document itself, since the on-screen filters are not carried into the output, and PDF is the format that becomes the permanent work paper.
scr_ap_customizing_and_running_the_appro.ifSkipped: Audit evidence is filed as unlabelled PDFs, and when a request comes back the team must re-run every report because none of them says what it covers.
gaap: SOC 1 — audit evidence must be identifiable and retained
AU-C 230 — audit documentation sufficient for an experienced reviewer
COSO 2013 — Principle 13, information retained in usable form
redFlags: PDFs filed with default titles and no period stated
Prompt on run enabled on a memorised report nobody answers correctly
Evidence retained only as on-screen views, never printed

scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report_col.purpose: Explains each column on the Approval History Audit report — transaction type as the grouping level, vendor, workflow name, the assigned approver role or user, the person who actually approved or declined (blank while pending), policy type and name, event date, comments and state.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report_col.outcome: A reader can tell, row by row, which rule applied, who was supposed to act and who actually did.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report_col.rootCause: The whole control test sits in the gap between two of these columns: the approver assigned by the policy and the user who actually approved. Where a transaction required two approvers under one policy, each appears as a separate row under the transaction — so a control exception looks like a missing row, not an error message, and only a reader who knows the column meanings will spot it.
scr_ap_approval_history_audit_report_col.ifSkipped: The report is filed as evidence without anyone reading it, and exceptions visible in the assigned-versus-actual comparison go unreported to management.

COSO 2013 — Principle 17, communicating control deficiencies

scr_ap_available_budget_page_3.purpose: The Available budget page as reached from the Spend management side of the Approval Workbench, where the tab set — Month, Year to date, Current year or job cost columns — again follows the line entry type chosen on the invoice, purchase order or subcontract.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_3.outcome: Budget context is available from the Spend management transaction path as well as from the approval queue, showing the same figures.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_3.rootCause: Two routes to the same page means two populations of users forming habits around it, and the Spend management users are the ones creating transactions rather than approving them. For them the Current year tab is the one that matters, because a service contract signed in March commits twelve months of spend that no monthly tab will ever reveal as a problem.
scr_ap_available_budget_page_3.ifSkipped: Transaction creators check a monthly figure before committing an annual contract, and the budget breach only appears in month seven when the line runs dry.
gaap: ASC 440-10 — commitments extending beyond the current period
COSO 2013 — Principle 13, information appropriate to the decision being made
redFlags: Annual contracts checked against a single month's budget

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.purpose: The Spend control budget check during subcontract creation as entered from the Spend management workbench, where the Remaining column explicitly excludes unapproved A/P invoice amounts and turns red in parentheses once the project is over budget.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.outcome: The person writing the subcontract sees a remaining figure whose exclusions are stated, not an optimistic one.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.rootCause: The exclusion of unapproved invoices is the detail that misleads on an active job. Late in a renovation there can be six figures of trade invoices sitting in the approval queue, all of which will hit 1410 Construction in Progress, and the Remaining column shows the budget as though none of them exist — so a subcontract written against it is committing money already spoken for.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.ifSkipped: Subcontracts are executed against budget that unapproved invoices have already consumed, and the job breaches its funded amount as soon as the queue clears.

ASC 360-10-30 — accumulation of capitalised project costs

redFlags: Remaining budget read without adding back the unapproved invoice queue

scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.purpose: The purchase order budget check reached from the Spend management workbench, showing Month and Year to date tabs for standard line items or the job cost budget for job cost line items, with over-budget amounts shown red and parenthesized.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.outcome: The buyer working inside Spend management gets the same budget view an approver would later see on the same PO.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.rootCause: The value here is that the buyer and the approver are looking at an identical figure. When a PO is queried later, the disagreement is never about the number — both parties saw the same Remaining — it is about whether the line entry type put the spend against the operating budget or the job budget, and that choice was made by the buyer on this screen.
scr_ap_viewing_the_available_budget_whil.ifSkipped: Buyer and approver reason from different budget bases, disputes over who authorised an overrun become unresolvable, and job costs land in operating accounts.

scr_ap_adding_a_new_transaction.purpose: The Add button on the Spend management workbench, which launches a new A/P invoice, purchase order information page or service contract information page with its associated service orders, depending on the transaction type selected.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_transaction.outcome: A new spend transaction is created from inside the workbench and enters the approval routing as soon as it is submitted.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_transaction.rootCause: Which type is chosen here determines what controls the transaction will ever face. An A/P invoice created directly bypasses any purchase order, so there is nothing to match against and no committed-cost record — the goods were ordered before anyone authorised them, and the approval at invoice stage is the first and only control over a spend decision already made.
scr_ap_adding_a_new_transaction.ifSkipped: Spend enters the system only as invoices after the fact, commitments are invisible, and three-way matching has nothing to match to.

ASC 440-10 — recording purchase commitments
ASC 405-10 — liability recognition on receipt
redFlags: Direct invoices for spend that should have carried a PO

scr_ap_editing_a_transaction.purpose: Edits an existing Spend management transaction through the Edit link in the Actions column, loading the A/P invoice, purchase order information or service contract information page for the item concerned.
scr_ap_editing_a_transaction.outcome: Transactions are corrected before or during routing, from one place, whatever their type.
scr_ap_editing_a_transaction.rootCause: Editing an item that is already in the approval queue is the specific danger: the approvers below have seen a version of the transaction that no longer exists, and depending on configuration the edit may not restart the route. An invoice approved at $4,900 and edited to $7,400 carries an approval chain describing a transaction that never existed at that amount.
scr_ap_editing_a_transaction.ifSkipped: Corrections are made by deleting and re-keying, losing the original submission date and the approval history that goes with it, or the wrong version is paid.

scr_ap_deleting_a_transaction.purpose: Removes a Spend management transaction through the Delete link, which appears only while the transaction's status is Draft — anything submitted, approved or posted cannot be deleted this way.
scr_ap_deleting_a_transaction.outcome: Abandoned drafts clear out of the workbench without touching anything that has entered the approval or posting chain.
scr_ap_deleting_a_transaction.rootCause: Restricting deletion to drafts is precisely what keeps the audit trail complete: the moment a transaction is submitted it becomes evidence about what someone asked for, and that has to survive even if the request was withdrawn. The residual risk is on the other side — drafts that are never deleted and never submitted sit in the workbench looking like pending work and distort every count taken from the queue.
scr_ap_deleting_a_transaction.ifSkipped: Stale drafts accumulate in the workbench, inflate apparent pending spend, and get resurrected and submitted months later against a closed budget period.

redFlags: Draft transactions older than a closed period still in the workbench

scr_ap_adding_a_change_order_for_a_trans.purpose: The CO link in the Spend management workbench Actions column, which opens either a change purchase order or a change subcontract form depending on the underlying transaction being amended.
scr_ap_adding_a_change_order_for_a_trans.outcome: A scope or value change is captured as its own approvable record attached to the original commitment.
scr_ap_adding_a_change_order_for_a_trans.rootCause: The change order exists so that the revised commitment, not the original, becomes the ceiling against which billing is checked — and on a subcontract that ceiling also drives the retainage calculation. A 10% retention on a contract whose value rose by $180,000 through unrecorded change orders under-withholds 2015 Retainage Payable by $18,000, which the owner discovers only when there is no retention left to hold against defective work.
scr_ap_adding_a_change_order_for_a_trans.ifSkipped: Vendors bill above the recorded contract value, retainage is withheld on the wrong base, and the lender's draw package will not reconcile to the approved project budget.

scr_ap_receiving_goods_for_a_transaction.purpose: Logs receipt against a purchase order from the Spend management workbench by entering quantities received per line, moving the PO to Received or Partially Received and enabling the Create invoice option while updating the received and open amounts.
scr_ap_receiving_goods_for_a_transaction.outcome: What physically arrived is recorded against the order, completing the third leg of the three-way match before any invoice is paid.
scr_ap_receiving_goods_for_a_transaction.rootCause: Receipt is the only independent confirmation that the property actually got what a vendor is billing for, and on a multifamily site it is entered by whoever signed for the delivery rather than by accounting. Where receiving is skipped and a full receipt is force-entered to unlock invoicing, the three-way match becomes a two-way match and short shipments are paid in full.
scr_ap_receiving_goods_for_a_transaction.ifSkipped: Invoices are paid on the order and the bill alone, short deliveries go unnoticed, and period-end accruals for received-not-invoiced goods have no quantity basis.
